topics.label: Introduction and lecture objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture within the cancer course and states what students should learn.

topics.label: Genetic origins and clonal evolution of cancer
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how mutations can produce cancer through clonal evolution, depending on cellular susceptibility and a permissive microenvironment.

topics.label: Environmental cancer risks and the bad-luck debate
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine the evidence and uncertainty surrounding environmental contributions to cancer rather than attributing its occurrence solely to chance or inherited predisposition.

topics.label: Infectious agents in cancer development
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how infections contribute to cancer, with Burkitt lymphoma illustrating the interaction between pathogens and oncogenic changes.

topics.label: Environmental carcinogens and mechanisms of DNA damage
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how environmental exposures produce DNA damage that can become mutations, often through the body's own metabolic processes.

topics.label: Tumour initiation and promotion
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics establish why mutagenic initiation may require a subsequent growth-promoting environment for tumours to develop.

topics.label: Tissue susceptibility and recap of carcinogenic mechanisms
topics.groupedBecause: The discussion of tissue-dependent susceptibility completes the account of carcinogenic mechanisms that the following recap consolidates.

topics.label: Methods for assessing carcinogenicity and exposure
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how evidence linking exposures to cancer can be obtained and what limits the conclusions drawn from that evidence.

topics.label: Closing summary and risk–benefit decisions
topics.groupedBecause: This closing draws together the lecture's conclusions about environmental cancer risks and their implications for everyday risk–benefit decisions.
